Charles Davis

Charles Davis was born in Goodman, Mississippi on May 20, 1933. He was educated in Chicago schools and first played the alto saxophone, soon to be followed by the tenor and baritone. Charles has played with most of the major figures in jazz, including Billie Holiday, Ben Webster, Clark Terry, Illinois Jacquet and the Thad Jones-Mel Lewis Big Band. His long association with Sun Ra began in 1954 and he joined the fellow baritone saxophonist Pat Patrick in creating Baritone Sax Retinue, an ensemble for six baris and rhythm section. He has also been associated closely with the music of Kenny Dorham and Tadd Dameron and has received a BMI Jazz Pioneer Award. Charles currently resides and works in New York City and frequently plays abroad.
Charles was interviewed by Monk Rowe, Director of the Hamilton College Jazz Archive, on August 23, 1997 at Hamilton College in Clinton, NY.
We are filming today for the Hamilton College Jazz Archive. It’s a pleasure for me to welcome as my guest Charles Davis, saxophonist.
Oh, thank you. Pleasure being here.
This isn’t your first trip through Upstate New York.
No, it’s not.
Do you have to travel outside New York a lot to keep working?
Well travel is part of working. Sometimes it’s to Utica. Recently I was up in Williamstown, Massachusetts, during six weeks of the summer, performing in a play.
You were performing in a play?
Well I was playing the saxophone, performing/playing the saxophone in the play. I didn’t have any actual lines.

That sounds interesting. As I was, for some reason today I was looking at the 802 Local book from, I think ‘95, and I got curious, and I added up all the saxophone players in Local 802, and it was over thirteen hundred players.
Oh, yeah, well that’s only the ones that’s in the Union.
I didn’t even think about that. So can I guess that there is extreme competition for work right in New York?
Well you could say that. Yes you can say it. Well if it’s something that’s an ongoing factor I guess in music, it’s always competition.
You’ve been in the music business — ‘54?
Around that time. Actually earlier, I think. I started playing, I started gigging a little bit in high school.
About what age were you, can you recall, when you decided that I think music is what I want to do for a living. © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-

Well I don’t know what age that was but music has always been a part of my life as a kid growing up, you know listening to records, Duke Ellington, Count Basie, Louis Jordan, all the big bands during the time.
Jazz and big bands, would you say that that was the popular music of the day when you were a kid?

Well, let me think, yeah. Well mostly it was swing during that time. Yeah, jazz, swing, whatever. It was hard to define when the main categories changed. You know, jazz, bebop, swing, avant garde and whatever. Now we have hip hop and whatever, but the names change.
Right. We have acid jazz.
Yeah. I don’t know what that is.
I haven’t figured it out either. Do you recall what you consider your first real professional gig that lasted a length of time? Mid-50s perhaps?
Yeah it was in the ‘50s. Well I first started out playing with Sun Ra around band-wise I think, as far as an established band, in the 50s.

When people hear the words Sun Ra, if they know at all who he is, I think most of us probably think of the kind of outlandish trappings that went along with all the things he did, but when you started with him in the mid-50s, what kind of music was he doing then?

Well even with all the outlandish trappings as you say, he still played the same thing. He had come out of Fletcher Henderson’s era and then as time progressed, the more the cosmic called him, the more he dealt with that situation. But he was like with Fletcher Henderson, and we were playing jazz, bebop, whatever. He always had a mythical essence to his music anyway.
Really? From the start, huh?
Yeah, from the start.
How did you guys deal with that? Did you think he was simply eccentric? Did you find it interesting or can you give me a clue as to how his fellow musicians ...

Well he was always a dedicated musician as far as I’m concerned. The other name categories you’re speaking of came from critics. You know that was the outside area. In the inside area, he was a dedicated musician. We used to rehearse and then he had singers he used to deal with, and then he used to write for a show band, for dancers in the show band in a club called Club DeLisa in Chicago. So he was always busy with music. So that was the main focus of his life was music.
And Chicago had a pretty healthy jazz and blues scene when you were growing up. It wasn’t your hometown, was it, but you ended up there? © Fillius Jazz Archive -3-
Well when I was a little kid I came to Chicago from Mississippi, like a lot of other people.
We’ve heard the name Club DeLisa mentioned a few times, and that that was a site where they would have a breakfast show or something?

Well that was Monday mornings, after Sunday nights. In Chicago during that time the clubs would close at four o’clock in the morning, five o’clock on Saturday morning, which was Sunday. So Sunday morning at four o’clock the club would close, and at six o’clock in the morning they would have the breakfast show from about six to eight or nine. Then after that you would go somewhere and jam, and it was playing music all the time, all the time. And at that time Joe Williams was working at the Club DeLisa. I know you had just mentioned Joe Williams and the Count Basie Band, but he was working at the Club DeLisa at the time.
Kind of an emcee for those things was he?
Emcee, vocalist, all around utility person.

Well, musicians at that time, what was the ... how did the racial make-up of what was going on in the music in those clubs? Was it a mixture? Was it reflective of what was happening in the general society at the time?

I guess so. It was a reflection of the times. Because at that time you had Local 208, which was the black local, and I’ve forgotten the name of the white Local, and then you had the south side and you had the north side. The south side was mostly black clubs, the north side was mostly white clubs. They kind of intermingled. You know people would come, at that time, although it was mostly like a segregated situation, but people would travel freely from one side to the other, especially in the music world. The music world had, for the most part, I know in the jazz world, it was more of an integrated society, just like it is now.

They seem to — I guess music has helped to lead the way in that respect. I remember recently when Jackie Robinson, they celebrated his 50th anniversary of breaking the color barrier in sports, but I think music preceded that.
Oh, yeah, definitely. That was with the Benny Goodman Trio, quartet, whatever, with Lionel Hampton, they kind of got over this — ‘39? And Billie Holiday with, which band did she play with?
Artie Shaw.
Artie Shaw’s band. So they had a lot of different situations where music was in the forefront of that society.
What was your educational experience in music?
Well the main focus of my education was Walter Dyett. I don’t know if you’re familiar with him. © Fillius Jazz Archive -4-
No.

Well this was from DuSable High School in Chicago, where a lot of musicians from Chicago were guided by this individual. Most musicians who came out of Chicago went to this high school. And he had a formula that musicians adapted to it, and became fairly successful behind it. I found that.
Did he teach jazz per se?

Well he wasn’t really a jazz teacher, he was a teacher. And then from that you dealt with what you wanted to deal with. Because we have some people that didn’t pursue the music, but they went on to being doctors and lawyers, and then we had some people that deal with classical aspects of music. So he was really a teacher. The jazz or whatever that you want to deal with in life it comes from you so you have to get it from the teacher and then you deal with the direction you want to go in.
In Chicago in those days, I mean there was a big blues scene too but was blues considered to be a kind of music that socially was not up to the level of other music?

Well it’s kind of hard for me to define that one. Because blues is always a part of your life, as far as that’s concerned. Well there are different levels of performance if you want to look at it that way.
I guess what I was thinking more of, was going to the blues clubs in Chicago, was that something that was not considered acceptable to do by certain parts of society?

Well that’s the same as jazz. Jazz had the same label. From when people would go slumming then would go to the speakeasies. So each faction of the music goes through the same change or the same encounter. But I mean today if you want to hear some blues you go to a blues club. If you want to hear some jazz you go to a jazz club. I mean that’s according to your religious beliefs now — which days you can go to the club.
In looking at your information in a couple of different books, starting in the late 50s you went through an amazing list of playing with people at the time — Billie Holiday and Ben Webster.
Yeah. Those were great times.
Tell me about those times.
Dinah Washington?
You had quite an association with Dinah Washington, right?

Yeah, well I worked for her about two, two and a half years. And also, I don’t know if it’s on there, Clarence Henry — speaking of blues — I first came to New York with Clarence Henry. You know, the “Frogman?”
The “Frogman.”

Yeah. I first came to New York with the “Frogman.” And then I went back, that was my first observance of the in-person view of the Statue of Liberty. And then I said well I’ve © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-

got to come back here. And then I came back with Dinah Washington. But while in Chicago I was lucky and fortunate enough to perform with Billie Holiday for about six months, on a local stint that she was dealing with in Chicago, with Billie Holiday and Ben Webster. So that was a pleasure, it was a real learning experience.
Was she — as a player, when you start working with vocalists, you need to start doing things perhaps in different keys than you’ve been used to doing them in, to match.

It was not that exceptional. Most vocalists I work with, it’s just normal keys, it was nothing exceptional. I mean it is different when you deal with vocalists that learn how to play off the guitar. Then that’s when your keys are exceptional.
Exceptional sharps, right?
Yeah.
What was your — did you have much big band experience over the years? With Sun Ra of course, but ...
I worked with Clark Terry, Thad Jones, the latest being Clifford Jordan. I was with his big band for a few years, playing the baritone, along with playing the tenor and alto in that band.
The baritone — your name comes up with baritone a lot.
Well that was the first --
Was that your first horn?
No that was the second horn. The first horn was alto.
Do you still like to play the baritone or --
On special occasions. I don’t really like to deal with the competitive aspects of trying to play in the big band and get a solo on the blues, so I’d prefer not to do that.
It seems like it must be a struggle sometimes. Harder to be heard on the baritone, because of the range perhaps?

No, my experience with the baritone, especially when you get to go through a sound check, is the guys will see the instrument and it’s large so they cut it down. I’ve had this problem for years. The altos and the tenors they’ll turn up and they’re loud. But the baritone they’ll turn down, so then you’ve got to huff and puff to be heard.
Hopefully some sound men will see this and take note.
Sometimes they’ll get it right, but the majority of times they’ll see the baritone and they’ll just turn everything on flat and low, and so that’s the problem.
Tell me about the baritone sextet.

Baritone Retinue. Well that was started with Pat Patrick and myself. This was years ago. But actually it was continuence of playing with Sun Ra because both of us used to play baritone with Sun Ra. In fact we recorded with two baritones with Sun Ra. © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-
Did he write out, how much of his music was actually written out, like big band charts, was it a lot of it?
With Sun Ra?
Yeah.
He wrote out everything. Stacks and stacks of music. He was always writing.
He had quite a diskography at the end of his life I guess. How much recording did you do with him?
I don’t remember. I really couldn’t say. I was in and out, in and out. I don’t have a list. Sometimes you look up and there’s some things that are out on records.
The music mostly came out on small labels at that time?
Yeah. Saturn and another one I remember recording for was Transition. That was a company that went out of business. But most companies, the small ones would go out of business.
Did you feel at the time recording with him and in those days that the compensation, the money you were being paid or not paid was worth it? From a recording standpoint?
Well I mean that’s a tricky question. It’s always worth trying to record and leave something for history. So that’s a situation where during those times you know all of the scales were lower anyway.
What was the union scale in the late ‘50s?
Oh, I don’t remember, I don’t know. Sometimes scale was 50, 70, I don’t know. I can’t recall exactly. Maybe you can research it from the union.
What year did you move to New York?
I actually moved to New York in 1959. That’s when I started playing with Kenny Dorham.
There’s a guy who wrote a few good times.
Yeah, quite a few.
In fact you played one last night, I think probably his most well known...
“Blue Bossa”?
Yeah. There was a little counter melody you guys were playing after you played the head? Where did that come from?
Well that’s a part of the song.
See most people don’t play that.
Yeah well that’s part of the song. I used to play it with him when we played it, but that’s part of the song.
What was New York like for a working musician when you moved there? Was it a process of breaking in and getting your name around? © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-
Yeah, that’s the same as it is now. But it was heaven, it was fantastic. It was a great place to be.
Do you still say that now, it’s a great place to be?
I still say it now. It’s a great place to be. There’s nothing like New York.
Do you have an agent that books work for you or do you mostly book your own engagements these days?
Well sometimes an agent calls you and sometimes — I don’t have a personal agent — God is my personal agent. But I’ve gotten calls from various agents from time to time.

If you had to place, I’m thinking of the effect of the church in jazz, or black music in general, do you have any views on how church music is affected — what you play or jazz or Gospel, that kind of thing.
How it’s affected what I play?
Yeah.
I don’t think it has affected what I play.

Could you describe the style of jazz you play? We were talking just now about labels, trying to put labels on things, and is it possible what you and Joe played last night, what you play down at Small’s when you visit the jam sessions there?

Well we’re still playing what’s given to us through the “bible” of bebop. Dizzy Gillespie and Charlie Parker and Fats Navarro and Kenny Dorham. I think this is — I don’t know if I’m playing it that well but this is what I’m attempting to do.
Would you consider bebop the hardest kind of jazz to play?
Yeah it is. And to develop it in that style is very, very difficult. And not run awry of the direction that you’re supposed to take in it.

Well this could be a hard question, but as I was listening to you last night and the rest of the group, a question I get a lot about music is, what’s a player thinking about? If you’re playing what some critics say “inside” or “outside” the changes, can you describe at all what you’re thinking about when you’re playing the changes on “All the Things You Are”? I told you it was a hard question.

What I’m thinking about is I hope I get through this and get out of it and thank you. I don’t know. It’s a hell of a mindset what to answer what you’re thinking at the time you’re doing it, because you’re thinking about what you’re dealing with and you’re saying “oh boy I wish I’d have practiced this better” or whatever. I don’t know, it’s just kind of hard to answer.
It is. It definitely is. Do you still think about the chord changes though? I mean that’s a pretty basic thing. © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-

Yeah well you have to relate to the chord changes and the sound. You know the chord changes are basic sound patterns so you have to find various ways to deal with the sound as you go through the chord patterns.

When you play, oh you did a blues number last night I guess “Straight, No Chaser” and to my ears, some of the changes you were playing were pretty adventurous. So how do you choose, I’m going to pursue this, this is a hard question I know, but how do you decide where to go, if you’re playing outside the change? Is there certain places you like to go that you can say I’m going to go up a major third, or is it less technical than that?

Well sometimes you go different places and nobody’s home, and you have to leave that and go somewhere else where they’ll let you in. So it’s a procedure. It’s something I’m working on, so I don’t want to sound ridiculous or redundant, but that’s the answer sometimes. It’s a process. Sometimes it works and sometimes it doesn’t.
And most of it happens on the gig instead of in your practice room.
Oh when you practice at home it’s great. I mean you’re the king of your room, until you bring it out and you find out that you’re just a peon.
Do you practice with accompaniment? Do you use any of these — I know nowadays they have all kinds of things that you can practice along to.

No, because when you’re playing you don’t have that. See if you have a play along and then you’re coming to play with somebody that’s strong and forceful and dynamic as Alvin Queen, then you’re not going to have the same effect, so you have to learn to deal with what you’re dealing with on the spot. You have to sometimes readjust. What you practice in your room with a play along is vastly different.

We were talking on the way up here about learning scales and learning what to do with them once you have them down. Are you a player who uses modes and that kind of approach in your playing or is it more what sounds good to your ear?
Well what is a mode?
Sometimes I wonder. Ice cream a la mode.

Well everything comes from the scale. So the more you about know about scales the more you know about the modes or whatever. And that’s just a scale, it’s one long ending sound. So after a while it’s just kind of monotonous, so you have to learn how to put other little things in the mode. Like you say, ice cream a la mode, so you just stick a little strawberry or cherry or whatever. It takes some adjusting just to play one thing all the time. And in doing that you have to find different things to play. Even John Coltrane, I mean he broke it up and found other things to play, even though it was based on one sound. But one sound has many sounds in it.
When you were, I suppose in your formative years of playing the saxophone, did you have major influences and people you liked to listen to and emulate perhaps? © Fillius Jazz Archive -9-

Oh, yeah, well I had many influences, still have influences as far as that’s concerned. One of the main influences, as it was then and it is now, is Charlie Parker. Lester Young, Ben Webster, Coleman Hawkins, on down to Sonny Rollins, John Coltrane, Clifford Jordan, John Gilmore, Gene Ammons, Johnny Griffin. See the list is long so there’s always influences. I grew up listening to Von Freeman
Wow, there’s a name you don’t hear that often. He has a son who plays also, right?
Yeah. So life is full of influences.
Did you see Charlie Parker in the clubs in New York at the time?
No, I saw him in Chicago on the dances. I didn’t want to see him in clubs. But dances and concerts I saw him.
Charlie Parker playing for dances?
Well that was a prerequisite during that time as far as my age would attest to, and that was the only thing that I could get into, 11, 12, 13 years old. I couldn’t get into clubs.
Dances were such a part of the swing music at that time.
Yes. Well that’s what a lot of it started from, dances. The bebop started out from dance music.
Do you think that the fact that that whole thing isn’t happening anymore is — how does it affect the music?

Well it’s according to where you are sometimes. A lot of times people will dance, but the clubs don’t allow you to dance, that’s the problem. When I used to play in Brooklyn people would get up and dance. It happens mostly say in Brooklyn or in Harlem or something like that, people will dance you know. Because it’s a tribal ritual to dance. So in Brooklyn and Harlem and whatnot, people will exuberate that spirit. A lot of times when they listen to the jukebox they’ll do it. But most sophisticated clubs now, you know, if you get up to dance they’ll stop you, you can’t do that. So that has its effect on the music, it has an effect as far as the music is concerned.
So you travel outside of the country on occasion?
Yes, on quite a few occasions. I’m on an occasion now to travel next week to Austria with Rodney Kendricks.
Is the reaction to jazz music any different overseas than here?

No I don’t think it’s any different. People react to music because they enjoy it. It’s a worldwide situation. People around the world love music. Some people love this type, that type, some people love jazz. So the reaction is not any different and sometimes in various parts of the world the reaction is better. I remember playing with Clark Terry’s band in Italy and we played a concert and the people enjoyed the music and everything was great. And we came out and we got on the bus and all these people were standing around the bus and I didn’t seem to understand why. And then we got on the bus and as © Fillius Jazz Archive -10-

we pulled off they gave us another round of applause. They stood around and waited until we were leaving and they gave us another round of applause. That was an astonishing event to me, just that the people would stop there and wait until you got on the bus and leave, just to give you another round of applause.
It sounds like a nice experience.
It is. It devastated me. I was flabbergasted, just to have people excited enough to want to do that.
When you go overseas do you sometimes get matched up with players from there, because you don’t always take a whole group?
Doing the singles, yeah, you deal with the rhythm section from other countries or from that country or people from other countries, as far as Europe is concerned.
Do you find that the musicians from those countries have basically learned the same jazz repertoire that we are familiar with?
Yes for the most part.
I was curious, last night you did “All the Things You Are” but what was that tune that you guys were playing?
It was a Kenny Dorham tune. The name of it was “Prince Albert.”
I knew I’d heard it but I could not place it.
Well it’s more Kenny Dorham.
I mean that’s a big part of becoming a performing jazz musician I would guess, just being able to play most of the night without music in front of you.

Yes well that’s true. Well then again, Monk, you have to remember that speaking of “Prince Albert” and “All the Things You Are” this is what was in the beginning as far as the repertoire was concerned. They started putting different melodies on standard tunes. So there was still the standard tune, but it was a bebop melody. So there was something there that the people could understand, even though they didn’t understand.
That they could still grasp the tune, the background of it, but it had something new and different over the top of it.

Yeah. So that was just “Prince Albert” which was made in 1949. It still sounds great today. So that was Kenny Dorham and James Moody with Max Roach’s band, and I think they made it in an air raid shelter in Paris in 1949 when Kenny Dorham and Max Roach went over with Charlie Parker. Paris. It was “Prince Albert” and there was another one called “Maxology” that Kenny Dorham wrote. So he’s been a prolific writer for some time.
You got honored by BMI, didn’t you?
Yes. It was in the mid-80s.
What was that for? © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-

Oh that was for being in BMI for 25 years. Yeah. There was a lot of us. I think Miles Davis was there that night, or during that afternoon, quite a few of us. There is a big picture of all of us. Miles Davis, myself, Ron Carter, a whole lot of musicians.

Do you find that the way the record industry is set up these days, do you feel that you get a fair slice of recordings and so forth that you do? Or are you kind of paid by the session and then that’s the end of it.

Well it’s according to your contract I guess. Every situation is different. I couldn’t answer for everybody. But it’s a little different. It’s best to get as much money as you can up front. Then you’re ahead of the game.
This could be another hard question, but can you think back to the music job that was perhaps the farthest away from what you envisioned yourself doing?

No, not really Monk, playing music is what I envision myself doing. As long as it’s music it’s great. Because there are various forms of music. Just because it’s not jazz doesn’t mean that it’s not worthwhile. Because when you first learn how to play you weren’t playing jazz, you were playing music. You know the C scale is in jazz and it’s in various forms of music, you know. So as long as it’s music it’s great.
Can I take you back to Chicago for another minute?
Okay.
There was a certain core of musicians at that time, did you ever associate with fellows like Milt Hinton?

No, he’s a little ahead of my time. But we have talked about Chicago on a number of occasions, because he informed me of some aspects of Walter Dyett. Walter Dyett used to teach at a school, in fact Walter Dyett taught him. He was in school with Nat King Cole and Dinah Washington, and his school burnt down and Walter Dyett went to DuSable as a temporary basis but he stayed. The school that burned down was Wendell Phillips, and they rebuilt it.
That’s right. I recall that name now.
And they rebuilt it, but at the time Milt Hinton and Nat Cole and Dinah Washington were going through the school.
Do you consider jazz to be, some people call it America’s classical music, or black classical music. Do you have a sense of how jazz is — your own personal sense of how jazz should be viewed?

It should be viewed with great respect. Myself personally, you know that’s my personal opinion. Because there’s nothing like it. I mean speaking of jazz, if you’re speaking about Dizzy Gillespie and Charlie Parker and Thelonious Monk, there’s nothing like it. It’s such a heck of a creative venue that nothing’s been created since then to equal it. It’s output, musically and emotionally and spiritually. © Fillius Jazz Archive -12-
Why do you think jazz, when it moved into the bebop era, that it lost a good portion of its audience?
Well it wasn’t bebop that lost the audience. When they turned to the cool jazz is when it lost its audience I think.
Why?
Well too cool.
Too cool.
It lost its sizzle. I think when it got too cool, the guys just became very cold as far as what they were doing. They were more into themselves then in dealing with the reality of their audience.
Well that’s a good statement. Musicians relating to their audience.
Yeah. Well that’s what it’s about.
Do you feel that your playing changes from one venue to the next?

Yes, it does, according to what you’re dealing with. I think it’s according to the way you are sometimes, what you’ll play. What motivates one audience doesn’t motivate the next audience so you have to keep that in mind.
Did you ever do much rhythm & blues playing in your career?
Let’s see, my Alzheimer’s just kicked in. Let’s see, well Clarence Henry was rhythm & blues. Clarence Henry. I played with quite a few rhythm & blues during the course of my career coming up.
Did you ever feel you had to really do that honking tenor sax thing?

Well that was a part of growing up. There was a lot of honking. John Coltrane had to honk. A lot of people had to honk. That was a tradition — honking and walking the bar. Sometimes you were forced to do it. Sometimes you were forced to do it at gun point. That’s in Chicago sometimes, people put a gun on you because they knew the solos so you couldn’t fool them.
They knew the solos?
The audience knew the solos. They paid that much attention to the records. They’d get the records, everybody knew the solos. So I know this happened to quite a few different people.
That they wanted to hear what was ...

They wanted to hear what was on the record. If you didn’t know it then you had to go home and learn it you know. You couldn’t fool ‘em. People wanted to hear “Flyin’ Home,” they wanted to hear the solo. They didn’t want you — if you couldn’t play it then you’d get off of that.
That’s some kind of pressure.
Yeah. © Fillius Jazz Archive -13-
They don’t teach that in school.

No, no, no, no, they don’t teach you that. And if they want you to walk the bar, they wanted you to walk the bar. You couldn’t say that wasn’t in your contract. It’s time to walk the bar, it’s time to walk the bar. That’s another thing, people wanted to see a show you know. When it was show time then you had to go out and put on a show, you couldn’t sit around and be that cool that you couldn’t put on a show saying that’s not my thing. So if it’s show time you get up and put on a show.
You want to get paid, you better do it.
Yeah. You may do it and don’t get paid. Guys put on a show laying on his back and playing the saxophone behind his back, anything to get through that scene.
Sounds like a tough town.
Yeah. But that was the tradition during that time.
Would you encourage young musicians to go into the field of jazz these days? What do you think is required besides being able to play?

Well endurance, you have to learn how to practice also. Because without the drudgery of practice, practice is not as pretty as what’s seen as a performer, or as you see a performer perform. Practice is a lonely art. It’s very demeaning sometimes when you have to practice something over and over and over and over just to get it.

Yeah it was, as we were saying, during this time you had to perform. They had clubs with what you called a bucket of blood. You had to go there and really bear down and get the house. “Flying Home” or whatever. Some of the other tunes were “Honky Tonk” and I know around Chicago Gene Ammons would have some hits out that you would have to know the solos. So I mean that was my world, because I had left Chicago at that time. So I mean whatever went down at the times, if that was a standard song, especially if it was a saxophone solo. You had to know it. And Charlie Parker had some solos out. “Cool Blues” people would play that at house parties and everybody could hum the solo. So if you had alto and you were playing “Cool Blues” and didn’t know the solo, people would get on you about it.
That’s really fascinating. It’s almost like today knowing the lyrics to rock songs I suppose.
Oh yeah. Some of them don’t really make sense to me, but whatever. Life is life and it continues on.
Any last words of wisdom for the typical saxophone student who says man, I’m going to be a jazz musician?

Well I would tell him to practice and learn his scales, and to be in for rejection the same as actors have to go through, all the successful actors and actresses, and whatever. People that deal with rejection in life, you have to learn to accept it. But you still have to practice © Fillius Jazz Archive -14-
your craft, whatever you do. And being for that, just keep your spirits high. That’s my best advice.

Sounds good to me. Well it’s been a pleasure to have Charles Davis here for our Hamilton College interviews, and I hope you have a great gig tonight, and I hope you have a smooth and wonderful trip to Austria.
Yes, Austria.
Thanks so much for your time.
Thank you for having me here. © Fillius Jazz Archive -15-

segments.title: Opening and working travel, New York competition
segments.summary: Welcome, travel for work, playing in a play, and competition among saxophonists in Local 802.

segments.title: Growing up on records and the big bands
segments.summary: Davis started gigging in high school; he grew up listening to Ellington, Basie and Louis Jordan, and talks about changing labels for the music.

segments.title: Early years with Sun Ra
segments.summary: Davis first played in an established band with Sun Ra; he says Sun Ra was a dedicated musician with a mythical essence from the start, writing for shows at Club DeLisa.

segments.title: Club DeLisa breakfast shows and Chicago nights
segments.summary: Davis came to Chicago from Mississippi as a child; he describes the Club DeLisa breakfast show, the jamming afterward, and Joe Williams working there.

segments.title: Race and integration in Chicago music
segments.summary: Segregated locals and south/north side clubs, with music more integrated; Benny Goodman, Hampton and Billie Holiday cited as pioneers.

segments.title: Walter Dyett and DuSable High School
segments.summary: Davis's main education was Walter Dyett at DuSable, a teacher rather than a jazz teacher.

segments.title: Blues and jazz and social respectability
segments.summary: Blues clubs and jazz had the same stigma, like slumming at speakeasies; now you go to the club that fits.

segments.title: Clarence Henry, Dinah Washington and Billie Holiday
segments.summary: Davis came to New York with Clarence 'Frogman' Henry, worked with Dinah Washington for two years and played with Billie Holiday and Ben Webster in Chicago; vocalists' keys.

segments.title: Big bands and the baritone saxophone
segments.summary: Big bands with Clark Terry, Thad Jones and Clifford Jordan; the baritone as second horn and the sound-check problem.

segments.title: Baritone Retinue, Sun Ra's music and recording pay
segments.summary: Baritone Retinue grew from playing with Pat Patrick in Sun Ra; Sun Ra wrote everything; small labels, and recording scale.

segments.title: Moving to New York and Kenny Dorham
segments.summary: Moved to New York in 1959 and began with Kenny Dorham; 'Blue Bossa' and New York as heaven.

segments.title: Booking work and church influence
segments.summary: No personal agent; church music has not affected his playing.

segments.title: Bebop style and thinking while playing the changes
segments.summary: Playing the bebop bible; the difficulty of bebop; playing changes, going outside, practice versus gigs, and modes.

segments.title: Modes and scales
segments.summary: Everything comes from the scale; modes need other things added, as Coltrane did.

segments.title: Influences, Charlie Parker and dances
segments.summary: Parker, Young, Webster and others as influences; seeing Parker at dances as a boy; dance and bebop and clubs.

segments.title: Playing overseas
segments.summary: Travel to Austria, audiences abroad, a Clark Terry band concert in Italy with applause at the bus, and European rhythm sections.

segments.title: Kenny Dorham's 'Prince Albert' and bebop repertoire
segments.summary: The tune 'Prince Albert' from 1949, new bebop melodies over standards.

segments.title: BMI honor, record deals and all music
segments.summary: BMI honor in the mid-80s, getting money up front, and valuing all music.

segments.title: Chicago schools: Milt Hinton, Dyett and Wendell Phillips
segments.summary: Milt Hinton and Dyett's history at Wendell Phillips with Nat Cole and Dinah Washington.

segments.title: Views on jazz, cool jazz and audiences
segments.summary: Jazz deserves respect; cool jazz lost the audience; playing changes with the venue.

segments.title: Rhythm and blues, honking and Chicago showmanship
segments.summary: Clarence Henry and R&B, honking and walking the bar, audiences who knew records' solos.

segments.title: Learning solos and the demands of practice
segments.summary: Practice as a lonely art, 'Flying Home', 'Cool Blues' solos people expected.

segments.title: Advice to young saxophonists
segments.summary: Practice scales, expect rejection and keep spirits high.

segments.title: Closing thanks
segments.summary: Thanks and goodbyes.
